oaxaca: Oaxaca is one of the 31 states of Mexico. It borders Guerrero, Puebla, Veracruz and Chiapas and has 533 kilometres of Pacific coastline. Several mountain chains meet there, so the terrain is among the most rugged in Mexico, with narrow valleys and canyons between ranges. Elevations run from sea level to 3,759 metres. Most Indigenous people live in the Central Valleys region, and 16 Indigenous peoples are officially recognised, of whom the Zapotecs and the Mixtecs are the most numerous. The isolating terrain is credited with helping these cultures survive better than most others in Mexico. The name comes from Huaxyacac, the Nahuatl name of a tree called guaje in Spanish, first applied to the Valley of Oaxaca by Nahuatl-speaking Aztecs.

Evidence of human habitation about 11,000 years BCE has been found in the Guilá Naquitz cave near Mitla. It holds some of the earliest known evidence of domesticated plants on the continent, including maize cob fragments, and was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010. By 2000 BCE agriculture was established in the Central Valleys, with sedentary villages. The diet of maize, beans, chocolate, tomatoes, chili peppers and squash lasted until the Spanish Conquest.

Spaniards reached Oaxaca very soon after the fall of Tenochtitlan. Zapotec leaders, hearing of the conquest, offered an alliance. Gonzalo de Sandoval, Francisco de Orozco and Pedro de Alvarado overcame the main Aztec stronghold four months after Tenochtitlan fell, and Hernán Cortés then sought the title of Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca. The state was created in 1824. During the Mexican War of Independence the area stayed loyal to the Crown and the capital remained in royalist hands until the war ended. Under Porfirio Díaz modernisation brought lighting, railways and new farming techniques, and its benefits went mostly to national and international corporations.

The capital is Oaxaca de Juárez, and the state has about 3.5 million people. The state's 570 municipalities include 418 governed by the system of usos y costumbres, which recognises local forms of self-governance. At least a third of the population speak Indigenous languages. The capital and nearby Monte Albán together are a World Heritage Site, and Mitla is another archaeological site of the valleys. Oaxacan cooking is known for its seven moles, and the Guelaguetza festival is held each July.
oda-clan: Oda Nobunaga first claimed that the family descended from the Fujiwara clan and later from Taira no Sukemori of the Taira clan. According to the clan's official genealogy, after Sukemori was killed at the Battle of Dannoura in 1185, his son Taira no Chikazane was entrusted to a Shinto priest at a shrine in Otanosho in Echizen Province and became the founder of the Oda.

Modern scholars find no evidence for the Taira descent. One theory holds that the family came from the Inbe clan, Shinto priests in Otanosho. Another suggests that Nobunaga claimed Taira ancestry to justify his seizure of power, drawing on a belief of the time that the Minamoto and Taira clans were destined to alternate in rule, though it has been questioned whether people then really held this belief.

In the middle of the Muromachi period the Oda served the Shiba clan, military governors of Echizen. When Shiba Yoshishige was appointed governor of Owari Province the Oda followed him there, and Oda Jōshō became deputy governor. After the Ōnin War the Shiba split into two warring factions, and from around 1466 the Oda did the same, with Iwakura Castle and Kiyosu Castle as the strongholds of the two sides.

As the Shiba declined, Oda Tatsusada rebelled against them in 1513, failed and was killed. Oda Nobutomo then made the Shiba his puppets. During the Tenbun period Oda Nobuhide overtook the main family, captured Nagoya Castle in 1538 and became the strongest lord in Owari. Oda Nobunaga, operating from Nagoya Castle, besieged and killed Nobutomo, his uncle, in 1555, and his branch then brought the whole province under its control before turning on the Imagawa, Saitō, Azai, Asakura and Takeda clans. Nobunaga was forced to suicide by his vassal Akechi Mitsuhide in the Incident at Honnō-ji in 1582.

The Oda did not disappear after Nobunaga. One branch became hatamoto, direct retainers of the Tokugawa shogun, and others ruled as minor daimyo. At the end of the Edo period these were the domains of Tendō in Dewa Province and Kaibara in Tanba Province, each rated at 20,000 koku, and Yanagimoto and Kaiju in Yamato Province, each at 10,000 koku. Under the daimyo Oda Nobutoshi the Oda of Tendō signed the pact that created the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei.

When the feudal domains were abolished in 1871, after the Meiji Restoration, the heads of all four houses were made viscounts in the new hereditary peerage. Descendants of the clan live throughout Japan today, mainly in the south and south-west.
odessa: Odesa lies in the Black Sea Lowland, on the southwestern shore of the Gulf of Odesa on the northwestern coast of the Black Sea. It is about 31 km north of the mouth of the Dniester, some 443 km south of Kyiv, and about 40 km east of the border with Moldova. It is a warm-water port. The city is sometimes called the Pearl by the Sea or the Southern Capital.

A large Greek settlement stood on the site no later than the middle of the 6th century BCE, and a necropolis of the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE has long been known. Some scholars believe it was a trading settlement founded by the Greek city of Histria, though whether the bay is the ancient Port of the Histrians is not settled. A Slavic port, Kotsiubijiv, is first mentioned in 1415 as part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. After 1529 the area, known as Khadjibey, belonged to the Ottoman Empire, which rebuilt the fortress there in the mid-18th century under the name Yeni Dünya, meaning New World, until its defeat in the Russo-Turkish War ended in 1792.

A decree of Catherine II in 1794 ordered a naval harbour and trading place at Khadjibey, and in 1795 it was officially renamed Odessa, after a Greek colony of Odessos that supposedly lay in the area. The first census, in 1797, counted 3,455 people, and by 1803 there were 9,000. Its first commercial bank opened in 1801. From 1819 to 1858 it was a free port.

In 1905 Odesa saw a workers' uprising supported by the crew of the battleship Potemkin, commemorated in Sergei Eisenstein's film The Battleship Potemkin, which includes a scene on the great stone staircase now known as the Potemkin Steps. In 1941 Romanian and German troops attacked the city, and the Siege of Odessa began on 5 August and lasted 73 days. In the 1991 referendum 85.38 per cent of Odesa Oblast voted for Ukrainian independence.

Odesa is the third most populous city of Ukraine and a major seaport and transport hub, with the Port of Odesa and the oil terminal at Port Pivdennyi. It is the administrative centre of Odesa Oblast. Its industries include shipbuilding, oil refining and chemicals. Its historic city centre, notable for its multiculturality and 19th-century urban planning, is a World Heritage Site.
odisha: Odisha lies in eastern India, bordering Jharkhand and West Bengal to the north, Chhattisgarh to the west and Andhra Pradesh to the south, with a coastline on the Bay of Bengal. Its coastal plain, which includes the lake Chilika, is rich in silt deposited by six major rivers: the Subarnarekha, Budhabalanga, Baitarani, Brahmani, Mahanadi and Rushikulya. The region is also known as Utkala, a name that appears in India's national anthem. The terms Odisha and Orissa derive from the ancient Prakrit Odda Visaya, found in the Tirumalai inscription of Rajendra Chola I, dated to 1025.

Acheulian tools of the Lower Paleolithic point to early human settlement. Kalinga is mentioned in ancient texts such as the Mahabharata and the Vayu Purana, and Baudhayana describes it as not yet influenced by Vedic traditions. Its borders coincide with those of modern Odisha. The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga in 261 BCE, the eighth year of his reign. His own edicts record about 100,000 people killed and 150,000 captured, and he is said to have turned to pacifism and Buddhism.

Cuttack became the capital of the region around 1135 under Anantavarman Chodaganga. In the 15th century Sarala Das, who translated the Mahabharata into Odia, called the land Odisha, and the inscriptions of Kapilendra Deva of the Gajapati Kingdom (1435–67) on temple walls in Puri use the same name. The British Indian government demarcated the modern boundaries, and the Orissa Province was established on 1 April 1936 from the Odia-speaking districts of Bihar and Orissa Province, the Madras Presidency and the Central Provinces. After 1948 the capital was Bhubaneswar.

Odisha is a state of India with over 41 million inhabitants. Odia, spoken by 82.70 per cent of the people at the 2011 census, is its official language and one of the classical languages of India. The Jagannath Temple at Puri, about 200 feet high, and the Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar are major Hindu pilgrimage sites, and part of the Konark Sun Temple survives.
odyssey: There is no consensus on when the Odyssey and the Iliad were composed. The Greeks began adopting a modified Phoenician alphabet in the 8th century BCE, and if the Homeric poems were among its earliest products they would have been composed towards the end of that century. Scholars agree that the epics developed in an oral tradition over hundreds of years. In the early twentieth century Milman Parry and Albert Lord showed that they have the marks of oral poetry, which lets even an illiterate poet improvise large poems. The poem was performed for audiences by a singer called an aoidos or rhapsode, and by the mid-6th century BCE it was part of the Greek literary canon.
In antiquity Homer's authorship was taken as true, though most scholars now assume that the two epics were composed independently, and the Homeric Question about their authorship still divides them.

The poem has 24 books and 12,109 lines of dactylic hexameter. It opens in medias res, with Odysseus, king of Ithaca, still absent ten years after the Greeks won the Trojan War. His journey home lasts another ten years, and all his crewmates are killed. At home 108 suitors court his wife Penelope, who says she will remarry when she has finished weaving a shroud for Odysseus's aged father Laertes, and each night secretly unweaves it. Athena sends his son Telemachus to seek news of his father, and he visits Nestor and Menelaus; this part, Books 1 to 4, is called the Telemachy.

Homecoming, nostos, is the central theme, with wandering, guest-friendship, testing and omens. The Phaeacians show exemplary guest-friendship, while Polyphemus and Calypso show poor guest-friendship. Back in Ithaca, Athena turns Odysseus into a beggar so that he can test who is loyal. Penelope tests him in turn by saying she will move their bed, which was made from a living tree, a fact that only the real Odysseus would know.

In the Byzantine Empire the epics remained school texts through the Middle Ages. Livius Andronicus made a Latin version, the Odusia, which became a school text for Latin students. The first printed edition in Greek appeared in Milan in 1488, and the first complete English translation in 1616. The epics formed the basis of education in the ancient Mediterranean, and Western humanists adopted that curriculum. A poll of experts by BBC Culture in 2018 named it literature's most enduring narrative.
ohio: Ohio takes its name from the Ohio River on its southern border, which comes from a Seneca word meaning good river, great river or large creek. The state covers about 116,100 square kilometres, with rolling glaciated plains across most of it, rugged unglaciated hills on the Allegheny Plateau in the southeast and 502 kilometres of Lake Erie coastline to the north. Nearly all of the river belongs to Kentucky and West Virginia, since a 1980 Supreme Court ruling placed the boundary at the northern low-water mark of 1792. The border with Michigan was adjusted after the Toledo War.

Spear points of the Folsom and Clovis types show that nomads lived in the Ohio Valley as early as 13,000 BCE. The settled Adena culture appeared between 1,000 and 800 BCE, and its best-known remnant is the Great Serpent Mound in Adams County. Around 100 BCE the Adena evolved into the Hopewell tradition, whose large earthworks survive at Marietta, Newark and Circleville and whose trading network spanned a third of the continent. The Hopewell disappeared from the valley about 600 CE. The Fort Ancient people, the Whittlesey culture and the Monongahela culture all disappeared in the 17th century, and their origins are unknown.

After the Beaver Wars of the mid-17th century the Iroquois Confederation claimed much of the Ohio country as hunting and beaver-trapping ground. Epidemics and war left it gradually repopulated by Algonquian peoples, many in multi-ethnic societies, who by the 18th century took part in the European fur trade. Ohio was organised as part of the Northwest Territory, defined in the Enabling Act of 1802, and was the first state admitted under the Northwest Ordinance and the first free state admitted after independence. Statehood came in 1803. Ohio University, founded in 1804, was its first college, and Oberlin College, founded in 1833, admitted African Americans in 1835 and women in 1837.

The capital and most populous city is Columbus; Cleveland and Cincinnati are the other major cities. The 2020 census counted 11,808,848 residents. Ohio is known as the Buckeye State and as the Mother of Presidents, having been the birthplace of seven presidents, and the Wright brothers designed and built their first successful airplane there. Among its surviving earthworks, the Serpent Mound and the Hopewell mounds remain the most visible traces of its early peoples.
oklahoma: Oklahoma covers 69,895 square miles (181,030 square kilometres) near the geographical centre of the 48 contiguous states. Most of it lies in the Great Plains, the Cross Timbers and the Interior Highlands, with ancient mountain ranges, prairie, mesas and eastern forests. It borders Texas, Kansas, Missouri, Arkansas, New Mexico and Colorado. Its southern and western boundary with Texas, the Red River and the 100th meridian, was first set in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819 between the United States and Spain.

Indigenous peoples were present by the last ice age. Ancestors of the Wichita, Tonkawa and Caddo lived in the area, and Spiro Mounds was a major Mississippian mound complex that flourished between 850 and 1450 CE. Plains Apache people settled the Southern Plains between 1300 and 1500. The Spanish expedition of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado crossed the region in 1541, and French explorers claimed it in the early eighteenth century. The Comanche and Kiowa entered from the west in that century, and the Quapaw and Osage moved into the east. The United States acquired the territory in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, and it was part of the Arkansas Territory from 1819 to 1828.

The name comes from the Choctaw words okla, meaning people, and humma, meaning red. Chief Allen Wright of the Choctaw Nation suggested it in 1865 during treaty negotiations over Indian Territory, imagining a state wholly for American Indians. It became the usual name of Oklahoma Territory and was officially approved in 1890, two years after that area was opened to settlers. The Indian Appropriations Act of 1889 authorised the Land Rush of 1889 that opened land formerly held by Indian nations; settlers who staked claims early gave the state its nickname, the Sooner State.

The northern border was set at the 37th parallel by the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which the Cherokee and Osage disputed until the Drum Creek Treaty of 1870. The Panhandle, once part of the Republic of Texas, remained a no-man's land until Oklahoma acquired it on gaining statehood in 1907. The first newspaper in the region, the Cherokee Advocate, appeared in 1844 in Cherokee and English.

Oklahoma City is the capital and largest city, and Tulsa the other main economic centre. Oklahoma is a constitutional republic with executive, legislative and judicial branches and 77 counties; its legislature has a 48-member Senate and a 101-member House. It has 38 federally recognised tribes with headquarters in the state, and 25 Indigenous languages are spoken there. The 2020 census counted 3,959,353 residents.
oliver-cromwell: Oliver Cromwell was born in Huntingdon on 25 April 1599 to Robert Cromwell and his second wife Elizabeth Steward. The family's estate came from an ancestor who married the sister of Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's chief minister, and it profited from the Dissolution of the Monasteries. He married Elizabeth Bourchier on 22 August 1620, a match that linked him to the Puritan gentry of Essex and the merchants of London. He sat for Huntingdon in 1628 and made little impression. He became a religious Independent in the 1630s, and afterwards believed his successes were the work of divine providence.

Returned for Cambridge to the Short and Long Parliaments in 1640, Cromwell raised a cavalry troop when civil war began in 1642. His cavalry were a major factor in the Parliamentarian victory at Marston Moor in July 1644. The Self-Denying Ordinance of 1645 forced members to choose between office and command, and Cromwell alone was kept in his. He led his wing at Naseby in June 1645, which smashed the King's main army. In 1648 he defeated the invading Scottish Engagers at Preston, and after the King's execution he commanded the campaign in Ireland in 1649 and 1650, then won at Dunbar on 3 September 1650 and at Worcester on 3 September 1651.

Barebone's Parliament voted itself out on 12 December 1653, and John Lambert's Instrument of Government made Cromwell Lord Protector. He was sworn in on 16 December in plain black clothing, without regalia, signed himself Oliver P and was addressed as Your Highness.

Cromwell died at Whitehall on 3 September 1658, probably of sepsis after a urinary infection and a bout of malarial fever. His son Richard succeeded him, and the Stuart Restoration followed in 1660. On 30 January 1661 his body was hanged at Tyburn, and his head was displayed on the roof of Westminster Hall until at least 1684.

His reputation remains debated. His report on Drogheda in September 1649 lists the killing of 3,000 military personnel and many inhabitants. Some historians argue that he acted harshly only against those in arms, while others note that the worst of the mass evictions and deportations of over 50,000 people to Bermuda and Barbados came under other generals after he left. Winston Churchill described him as a military dictator, while others view him as a hero of liberty.
oman: Oman lies between latitudes 16 and 28 degrees north. A gravel desert plain covers most of the centre, with the Hajar Mountains along the north and the Dhofar Mountains along the south-east coast, where the main cities stand: Muscat, Sohar and Sur in the north and Salalah in the south. The peninsula of Musandam, on the Strait of Hormuz, is an exclave cut off from the rest of Oman by the United Arab Emirates. The climate is hot and dry inland and humid on the coast, and the Dhofar Mountains receive monsoon rain from late June to late September.

Stone tools found at Al Aybut Al Awal in Dhofar, dated to about 106,000 years ago, support the view that early human groups moved from Africa into Arabia in the Late Pleistocene. The Bronze Age Umm an-Nar and Wadi Suq periods left many remains, including monumental architecture. Sumerian tablets of about 2300 BCE call the region Magan, a source of copper and diorite for Mesopotamia, and the Magan civilisation is said to have lasted until 550 BCE. The oldest known written mention of the name Oman comes from a tomb at Mleiha, dated to about 220 BCE.

From the 17th century Oman became a regional power, expelled the Portuguese from its coastal possessions and built an empire that competed with the Portuguese and British in the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean. In the 19th century its influence reached across the Strait of Hormuz and south to Zanzibar. The Al Bu Said dynasty has ruled continuously since 1744. In the 20th century Oman came under British influence while remaining formally sovereign, and after the Dhofar rebellion and the coup of 1970 it became the modern state under Qaboos bin Said.

Oman is a sultanate with its capital and largest city at Muscat. Arabic is the official language and Islam the state religion. The Basic Statute of the State, issued in 1996, serves as its constitution. The country has about 5 million people and belongs to the United Nations, the Arab League and the Gulf Cooperation Council.
omar-khayyam: Omar Khayyam was born in 1048 at Nishapur, a metropolis in the province of Khorasan in the Seljuk Empire, of Persian stock. His full name was Ghiyath al-Din Abu al-Fath Umar ibn Ibrahim Nishapuri. It has often been assumed, though it is open to doubt, that his forebears were tent-makers, since khayyam means tent-maker in Arabic. The historian Bayhaqi, who knew him personally, gave the details of his horoscope, which modern scholars used to establish his date of birth as 18 May 1048. Khayyam was known in his lifetime as a mathematician, and he considered himself a student of Avicenna.

In 1074-5 Sultan Malik-Shah commissioned Khayyam to build an observatory at Isfahan and to reform the Persian calendar. A panel of eight scholars worked under his direction, making large-scale astronomical observations and revising the astronomical tables. The calendar fixed the first day of the year at the moment the centre of the Sun crosses the vernal equinox, marking Nowruz. It was named the Jalali calendar in the sultan's honour and inaugurated on 15 March 1079. It used a 33-year cycle of 25 ordinary years of 365 days and 8 leap years of 366 days, and remained in use across Greater Iran from the 11th to the 20th centuries. The observatory fell into disuse after Malik-Shah died in 1092.

His surviving mathematical works include a commentary on Euclid's postulates, completed in December 1077, and a Treatise on Algebra, most likely completed in 1079. He seems to have been the first to conceive a general theory of cubic equations and to solve every type of cubic geometrically, so far as positive roots are concerned, using conic sections. In treating the parallel axiom he refuted earlier attempts at proof and considered the acute, obtuse and right angle cases of what is now called the Khayyam-Saccheri quadrilateral. He also wrote on Archimedes' principle, on music theory, and in philosophy, where he wrote on existence, free will and determinism.

A tradition attributes quatrains, or rubaiyat, to him. The earliest allusion to his poetry comes from the historian Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, a younger contemporary, and the earliest quatrains are quoted in works of about 1160 and 1230. Because quotations in 13th- and 14th-century texts are of doubtful authenticity, sceptical scholars point out that the whole tradition may be pseudepigraphic. Edward FitzGerald's English translation of 1859, at first unsuccessful, became extremely well known by the 1880s and led to Omar Khayyam Clubs and a cult of the Rubaiyat.
omsk: Omsk lies in the south of the West Siberian Plain, on the banks of the north-flowing Irtysh at its confluence with the Om River, which gives the city its name; in the dialect of the Baraba Tatars the hydronym means the quiet one. It stands about 450 km north of Astana and 2,230 km east of Moscow. Omsk is the junction of the northern and southern branches of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and its river port gives access to the waterways of the Irtysh and the Ob.

The fortress at Omsk arose from the need to secure the trade route to China. The Siberian governor, Prince Matvey Gagarin, obtained the tsar's consent in May 1714 to build fortresses along the Irtysh. By the end of 1716 the first fortress, an earthen pentagon with stores, barracks and officers' houses, stood at the mouth of the Om. Omsk was granted town status in 1782, and in 1822 it became the administrative capital of Western Siberia. As the frontier receded the town became a major centre of Siberian exile; Fyodor Dostoyevsky served his sentence in an Omsk prison from 1850 to 1854. The Trans-Siberian Railway of the 1890s made it a logistic hub.

After the October Revolution the Provisional All-Russian Government was established in Omsk in 1918 under Admiral Kolchak, and the city was proclaimed capital of Russia, its central bank keeping the former empire's gold reserves. The Red Army forced Kolchak to retreat east to Irkutsk, and Bolshevik forces entered Omsk in 1919. The Second World War gave the city new life, because industry was evacuated there from the front. In the 1950s the development of Siberian oil led to a refinery complex, now the largest in Russia.

Omsk is the administrative centre and largest city of Omsk Oblast and has more than a million inhabitants. It is the third largest city in Siberia, after Novosibirsk and Krasnoyarsk. It is the seat of the bishop of Omsk and Tara.
onake-obavva: Obavva belonged to the Holaya community. Her husband, Kahale Mudda Hanuma, was the guard of a watchtower in the rocky fort of Chitradurga, which the troops of Hyder Ali besieged during the reign of Madakari Nayaka. As the story is told, a chance sighting of a man entering the fort through a hole in the rocks gave Hyder Ali the plan of sending his soldiers in by the same way.

The guard on duty near the hole had gone home for his meal. When he wanted water, Obavva went to fetch it in a pot from a pond near the hole, halfway up the hill, and there saw the soldiers trying to enter. She struck each on the head with the pestle as he came through and quietly moved the body aside, so that those behind suspected nothing. Mudda Hanuma returned to find her standing with the bloodstained pestle among the enemy dead.

She was found dead later the same day, either from shock or killed by enemy soldiers. Her act saved the fort on that occasion, but Madakari Nayaka could not withstand Hyder Ali's attack in 1779, when Chitradurga was lost to him.

In Karnataka she is honoured beside Abbakka Rani, Keladi Chennamma and Kittur Chennamma as one of the foremost women warriors of the state. Since 2021 the Government of Karnataka has celebrated 11 November as Onake Obavva Jayanti. A sports stadium in Chitradurga bears her name, and a statue of her by the sculptor Ashok Gudigar stands in front of the District Commissioner's office there. Her deed is shown in a song sequence of the film Nagarahavu, directed by Puttanna Kanagal, in which the actress Jayanthi played her, and in the 2019 Kannada film Chitradurgada Onake Obavva, with the actress Tara in the role.
one-thousand-and-one-nights: One Thousand and One Nights is a collection of Middle Eastern folktales compiled in Arabic during the Islamic Golden Age. It was collected over many centuries by various authors, translators and scholars across West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia and North Africa. Some tales go back to ancient and medieval Persian, Arabic and Mesopotamian literature, but most were originally folk stories of the Abbasid and Mamluk eras. The frame story comes from the Pahlavi Persian work Hezār Afsān, meaning A Thousand Tales, which in turn relied partly on Indian elements. The earliest mentions of the Nights describe it as an Arabic translation from that Persian book.

The tenth-century Fihrist of Ibn al-Nadim in Baghdad mentions Hezār Afsān. One of the oldest Arabic manuscript fragments, a few handwritten pages from Syria dating to the early ninth century, was discovered by the scholar Nabia Abbott in 1948. It bears the title Kitab Hadith Alf Layla, The Book of the Tale of the Thousand Nights.

In the frame story the king Shahriyar is told tales by his wife Scheherazade, one for each night of storytelling, and some stories are framed within others while some are self-contained. The bulk of the text is in prose, with verse used for songs, riddles and heightened emotion. If a canonical text with every story in a fixed order ever existed, it no longer survives. Editions range from a few hundred nights to 1001 or more, and the corpus now comprises more than 550 tales. Variants of the ending agree that Shahriyar pardoned Scheherazade and spared her life.

The Nights use the frame story and the story within a story, techniques with roots in earlier Persian and Indian storytelling such as the Sanskrit Panchatantra, and its tales also make use of foreshadowing, repetition and the device of the unreliable narrator.

Four printed Arabic editions, all of the 19th century, are taken as canonical: Calcutta I, Bulaq, Breslau and Calcutta II. Calcutta I was printed by the British East India Company in 1814 to 1818. The first European version, in French, was made by Antoine Galland between 1704 and 1717 in twelve volumes. It included tales such as Aladdin's lamp and Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves that appear in none of the original manuscripts; Galland said he heard them from the storyteller Hanna Diyab. The first English edition, of about 1706 to 1721, gave the work the title The Arabian Nights' Entertainments.
ontario: Ontario is the southernmost province of Canada, bordered by Manitoba to the west, Hudson Bay and James Bay to the north and Quebec to the east and northeast. To the south lie the United States, from Minnesota to New York. Almost all of its 2,700-kilometre international border follows rivers and lakes of the Great Lakes drainage system. The Canadian Shield covers over half of the land area and is rich in minerals but mostly unsuited to farming, while most people and most arable land are in Southern Ontario. The province has about 250,000 freshwater lakes.

Paleo-Indians first settled the land about 11,000 years ago. French exploration followed the founding of Quebec in 1608, and the French named the region the Pays d'en Haut, the Upper Country, a dependency of Canada that existed for defence and trade rather than settlement, in which Indigenous peoples were the vast majority of the population.

In 1782–1784 about 5,000 United Empire Loyalists entered the land after the American Revolution, and Britain granted them 200 acres each. The British also resettled displaced Iroquois at the Six Nations reserve at the west end of Lake Ontario in 1784. Upper Canada was created in 1791, and John Graves Simcoe was appointed its first lieutenant governor in 1793. After rebellions, Lord Durham recommended responsible government and the reunion of Upper and Lower Canada. The colonies were merged as the Province of Canada, with Upper Canada becoming Canada West. Responsible government was achieved in 1848, and heavy immigration in the 1840s more than doubled its population by 1851.
The name Ontario was adopted at Confederation in 1867. After Canada acquired Rupert's Land, a boundary dispute led to the province's northern limit being set at the 51st parallel north.

Ontario is the most populous province of Canada, with over 14 million people, and the second-largest by total area after Quebec. Its capital, Toronto, is the country's most populous city, and Ottawa, the national capital, lies within its borders. Its legislature is the Legislative Assembly of Ontario, established by the British North America Act of 1867. The Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto, founded in 1912, is the largest museum in Canada. The name is thought to have Indigenous origins, either Ontarí:io, a Huron word meaning great lake, or skanadario, beautiful water.
opec: In 1949 Venezuela invited Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia to exchange views and explore closer communication among petroleum-exporting nations, as the world recovered from World War II. In February 1959 the multinational oil companies unilaterally cut their posted prices for Venezuelan and Middle Eastern crude oil by 10 per cent. Weeks later, at the Arab League's first Arab Petroleum Congress in Cairo, Saudi Arabia's Abdullah Tariki met Venezuela's observer Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo.

The Baghdad Conference of 10 to 14 September 1960 was held at the initiative of Tariki, Pérez Alfonzo and the Iraqi prime minister Abd al-Karim Qasim. Representatives of Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela met to discuss raising the price of their crude oil and answering the companies' unilateral actions, despite strong United States opposition. The organisation was founded on 14 September 1960.

In a series of steps in the 1960s and 1970s OPEC restructured the world's oil production in favour of producing states and away from an oligopoly of Anglo-American firms known as the Seven Sisters. Coordination within OPEC made it easier for states to nationalise oil production and set prices in their favour. The oil market was tight in the early 1970s, which lowered the risk of nationalisation, and a wave of nationalisations followed in Libya, Algeria, Iraq, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. In 1973 members unilaterally raised oil prices, which led to the 1973 oil crisis.

After 1973 OPEC added to its goals the selling of oil for the socio-economic growth of poorer nations, and the OPEC Special Fund was established in January 1976. After prices approached US$40 a barrel in 1979 and 1980, industrial nations turned to coal, gas and nuclear power and developed non-OPEC oilfields in Siberia, Alaska, the North Sea and the Gulf of Mexico.

The OPEC Conference is the supreme authority and consists of delegations normally headed by the oil ministers of member countries. The secretary general is its chief executive. It ordinarily meets at the Vienna headquarters at least twice a year, and generally works by unanimity and one member, one vote, with each country paying an equal fee. Saudi Arabia, the largest exporter, has enough capacity to act as the swing producer and is regarded as the de facto leader.

Members differ widely in export capacity, costs and reserves, so agreeing on policy is often difficult. Economists often cite OPEC as a textbook example of a cartel, though some sources take a broader view. Its formation marked a turning point toward national sovereignty over natural resources.
orleans: Orléans stands about 120 kilometres south-west of Paris, at the northern bend of the Loire, where the river curves west towards the Atlantic. It lies within the stretch of the Loire valley that UNESCO inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000. Because the city sits at the river's most northerly point, it is the Loire's closest point to Paris. The river was formerly an important route of navigation and trade, and it is at the heart of the city's foundation in the second century BCE as a centre of trade.

Cenabum was a stronghold of the Carnutes, where the Druids held their annual assembly, and Julius Caesar destroyed the city in 52 BCE. In the late 3rd century CE it was renamed civitas Aurelianorum, possibly in honour of a Roman emperor of the Aurelian name, and this evolved into Orléans. In the Merovingian era it was capital of the Kingdom of Orléans after Clovis I divided his kingdom. Under the Capetians it became a county and then a duchy held in appanage by the house of Valois-Orléans, which later reached the throne through Louis XII and then Francis I. In 1108 Louis VI was crowned in its cathedral, one of the few French kings crowned outside Reims.

Few bridges crossed the Loire, and Orléans had one, which helped make it one of the three richest cities of medieval France, with Rouen and Paris. The battle at the châtelet des Tourelles on 8 May 1429 allowed Joan of Arc to enter the city and lift the siege by the Plantagenets. Every first week of May since 1432 the city has held the Johannic Holidays in her honour.

Orléans is the prefecture of the Loiret department, in the region of Centre-Val de Loire, with 116,357 inhabitants in 2023. A university was created there in 1306 by Pope Clement V and re-founded in 1966 as the University of Orléans. A Gallo-Roman wall of the 4th century survives beside the cathedral. The city gave its name to the Île d'Orléans in Quebec and, through the regent, the duke of Orléans, to New Orleans.
osaka: Osaka is a designated city in the Kansai region of Honshu. Its west side is open to Osaka Bay, and it is otherwise surrounded by more than ten satellite cities, all in Osaka Prefecture except Amagasaki, in Hyōgo Prefecture, to the northwest. When Osaka was established as a city in 1889 it occupied roughly the area of today's Chuo and Nishi wards, 15.27 square kilometres, which grew by incremental expansions into today's 222.30 square kilometres. The largest was a single expansion of 126.01 square kilometres in 1925.

Central Osaka is roughly divided into the downtown and uptown areas of Kita, meaning north, and Minami, meaning south. Kita holds the Umeda district, a major business and retail hub, and Minami, which is in Chūō Ward, holds the Namba and Shinsaibashi shopping areas and the Dōtonbori canal entertainment area. The business districts between them, known as Semba, house the regional headquarters of many large banks and corporations.

In the Jōmon period, about 7,000 BCE, present-day Osaka was mostly submerged, and the Uemachi Plateau formed a peninsula 12 kilometres long and 2.5 kilometres wide, separating Kawachi Bay from the Seto Inland Sea. It is considered one of the first places where inhabitants of Japan settled, because of its fresh water and vegetation and because it could be defended. The earliest evidence of settlement is the Morinomiya ruins in Chuo-ku, with human skeletons, shell mounds, arrowheads, stone tools, fishing hooks and crockery. Permanent habitation on the plains grew in the Yayoi period (300 BCE to 250 CE) as rice farming became popular.

By the Kofun period (300 to 538) the area had developed into an important regional port, and in the seventh and eighth centuries it served briefly as the imperial capital. It continued to flourish in the Edo period (1603 to 1867) and became known as a centre of Japanese culture. After the Meiji Restoration it expanded greatly and industrialised rapidly, and it was the industrial hub of the Meiji and Taishō eras.

Osaka is the capital and most populous city of Osaka Prefecture, with an estimated 2.8 million people. It is the largest component of the Keihanshin metropolitan area. Panasonic and Sharp are headquartered there, and it is home to the Osaka Exchange. Landmarks include Osaka Castle, Dōtonbori, Tsūtenkaku in Shinsekai, Sumiyoshi Taisha Grand Shrine and Shitennō-ji, one of the oldest Buddhist temples in Japan.

The name Ōsaka means large hill or large slope. The oldest written evidence for it dates to 1496, and it is unclear when it gained prominence over Naniwa. The kanji 阪 became the official form in 1868 after the Meiji Restoration, replacing 坂, which was disliked because it can be read as samurai rebellion.
osama-bin-laden: Osama bin Laden was born into the wealthy bin Laden family of Saudi Arabia. His exact date of birth is unknown: Saudi men of his generation often did not know theirs, and in a 1991 interview he gave the month of Rajab in the Islamic year 1377, which could be 1957 or 1958. Researchers generally agree that he was born in Riyadh. He was raised a Sunni Muslim in the Athari school of theology.

In 1979 the Soviet Union occupied Afghanistan, and bin Laden left college to go to Pakistan with Abdullah Yusuf Azzam to help the Afghan mujahideen. He likely did so with the support of the Saudi government. In 1984 he co-founded Maktab al-Khidamat to recruit foreigners to the resistance, and in 1988 he founded al-Qaeda.

After the Soviet withdrawal he returned to Saudi Arabia, where many praised him as a hero of jihad. During the Gulf War he offered the royal family a mujahideen force, but they accepted 500,000 U.S. troops, and he was expelled in 1991. He went to Afghanistan and then to Sudan. In 1993 al-Qaeda bombed the World Trade Center complex in New York City. Expelled from Sudan, he returned to Afghanistan in 1996, and al-Qaeda allied with the Taliban. In 1996 and 1998 he issued fatwas declaring war on the United States, and in 1998 al-Qaeda bombed U.S. embassies in East Africa.

The attacks of 11 September 2001, planned mainly by bin Laden and Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, were carried out by nineteen al-Qaeda members who hijacked four passenger planes. They struck the World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon, and one plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. The attacks directly killed 2,977 victims. Bin Laden did not unambiguously take responsibility until a video of 2004.

After the United States invaded Afghanistan and deposed the Taliban, bin Laden relocated to Pakistan, and in 2005 he moved into a compound he had built at Abbottabad. U.S. intelligence found it in 2010, and on 2 May 2011 he was killed inside it in a raid by U.S. Navy SEALs, code-named Operation Neptune Spear. Ayman al-Zawahiri succeeded him as emir of al-Qaeda. Polls show that Muslims at large have a negative view of bin Laden, while many Islamists consider him heroic. Elsewhere he is overwhelmingly seen as a symbol of terrorism and mass murder.
oslo: Oslo occupies an arc of land at the northernmost end of the Oslofjord. The fjord, which the Nesodden peninsula nearly bisects opposite the city, lies to the south; in every other direction the city is surrounded by green hills and mountains. Within its limits are 40 islands, the largest being Malmøya, and 343 lakes, of which Maridalsvannet is the largest and a main source of drinking water.

In the Viking Age the area lay in Viken, the northernmost province of Denmark, and control over it shifted between Danish and Norwegian kings until Denmark gave up its claim in 1241. According to the Norse sagas Oslo was founded around 1049 by Harald Hardrada, but archaeologists have found Christian burials from before the year 1000, evidence of an earlier urban settlement, and the city marked its millennium in 2000. It became a bishopric in 1070. Under Olaf III (1067–1093) it was a cultural centre for Eastern Norway, and Hallvard Vebjørnsson, its patron saint, is shown on the city's seal.

Hovedøya Abbey was built in 1174, and churches and abbeys came to own large tracts of land. At the end of the 12th century Hanseatic League traders from Rostock moved in and gained major influence. Oslo became a capital under Haakon V around 1300, but personal unions with Denmark from 1397 to 1523 and from 1536 to 1814 reduced its standing.

A fire destroyed the city in 1624, during the reign of Christian IV, and a new city was built closer to Akershus Fortress and named Christiania in his honour. The old site east of the Aker river remained as a suburb called Oslo. Christiania was the capital of Norway during the union with Sweden from 1814 to 1905; government usage spelled the name Kristiania from 1877, and the municipality adopted that spelling in 1897. In 1925 the name Oslo was given to the whole city, and the old suburb became Gamlebyen. In 1948 Oslo merged with the much larger municipality of Aker, creating the present city.

Oslo is the capital of Norway and the seat of its government and parliament, the Storting. It is both a municipality and a county, with 724,290 inhabitants in the municipality on 1 January 2025 and roughly 1.5 million in the wider urban region. Frogner Park holds the sculptures of Gustav Vigeland, and the Bygdøy peninsula is the site of the Fram Museum, the Viking Ship Museum and the Kon-Tiki Museum.
ottawa: Ottawa lies in the south-eastern part of the province of Ontario, at the confluence of the Ottawa River and the Rideau River, with a third major river also meeting within the city. Across the river is Gatineau, Quebec, and the two form the Ottawa-Gatineau metropolitan area and the National Capital Region. The name was chosen in 1855 after the Ottawa River, whose name comes from the Algonquin adawe, meaning to trade. In modern Algonquin the city is called Odàwàg. The city's land area is 2,788.2 square kilometres.

The Ottawa Valley became habitable about 10,000 years ago, after the Champlain Sea drained. The first evidence of people there is spearpoints dated 8,000 to 8,500 years before the present. Settlements are documented at the mouth of the Gatineau River from 3,000 to 3,500 years ago, suggesting that the Algonquin people foraged, hunted, fished and traded there. The three rivers made the area an important route for trade and travel. In 1610 Étienne Brûlé became the first documented European to navigate the Ottawa River, and three years later Samuel de Champlain wrote about the waterfalls and the Algonquin people he met.

The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, incorporated in 1850 and renamed Ottawa in 1855. In 1968 the Region of Ottawa-Carleton was formed as a two-tier municipality out of eleven townships, two cities and three villages, and in 2001 it became a single-tier city. As the national capital it has hosted events such as the first visit of a reigning Canadian sovereign, King George VI, to his parliament on 19 May 1939, the first raising of the new national flag on 15 February 1965, and the centennial of Confederation on 1 July 1967. Queen Elizabeth II issued the royal proclamation of the Constitution Act there on 17 April 1982.

Ottawa is the capital of Canada and the seat of the federal government. It houses the Parliament of Canada, the Supreme Court, the residence of the Governor General at Rideau Hall, and the Office of the Prime Minister. The 2021 census counted 1,017,449 people in the city and 1,488,307 in the metropolitan area. Its institutions include the University of Ottawa, Carleton University, founded in 1942, the National Arts Centre and the National Gallery of Canada. The Ottawa Public Library was created in 1906 as part of the Carnegie library system.
otto-von-bismarck: Otto von Bismarck was born on 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen, a noble estate west of Berlin in Prussian Saxony. His father was a Junker estate owner and former Prussian officer, and his mother came from a family of senior civil servants in Berlin. In 1816 the family moved to its Pomeranian estate at Kniephof. He studied law at the University of Göttingen from 1832 to 1833 and then at the University of Berlin, and he knew English, French, Italian, Polish and Russian.

Others took him for a typical backwoods Prussian Junker, an image he encouraged by wearing military uniforms. In 1847 he was chosen as a representative to the newly created Prussian legislature, the Vereinigter Landtag, where he gained a reputation as a royalist and reactionary with a gift for stinging rhetoric.

In 1861 Wilhelm became King of Prussia and soon clashed with the Landtag, which in 1862 refused funds for a reorganisation of the army. On the advice of Albrecht von Roon he appointed Bismarck Minister President and Foreign Minister on 23 September 1862. Bismarck argued that the constitution had a legal loophole where a budget failed to pass, and kept collecting taxes on the basis of the 1861 budget for four years. With Roon's reorganisation of the army and Moltke's military strategy, his diplomacy brought wars with Denmark, Austria and France, and the creation of the German Empire.

In 1871 he was made a prince and the first Imperial Chancellor of the German Empire, while keeping his Prussian offices, so that he had nearly complete control of domestic and foreign policy. That year he began the Kulturkampf in Prussia, partly from fear of papal power; it failed, and the Catholics formed the Centre Party. His diplomacy aimed to keep Germany's position in a peaceful Europe.

Wilhelm I died in 1888 and Frederick III after 99 days. The new emperor, Wilhelm II, wanted rapid expansion and a larger German place in the sun. The final split came over Bismarck's attempt to make the Anti-Socialist Laws permanent. Wilhelm refused to open his reign with a bloody campaign against his own subjects, and Bismarck was forced to resign. Historians have praised him as the statesman who united Germany, and have also criticised his authoritarian rule.
ottoman-empire: As the Rum Sultanate declined in the 13th century, Anatolia became a patchwork of independent Turkish principalities known as the Anatolian Beyliks. One of them, in the Bithynia region on the Byzantine frontier, was led by Osman I, a figure of obscure origin from whom the name Ottoman is derived. His early followers were Turkish tribal groups and Byzantine renegades, not all of them Muslim. A Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Bapheus in 1302 contributed to his rise.

How the early Ottomans came to dominate their neighbours is not well understood, because sources are lacking. The Ghaza thesis, popular in the 20th century, credited their success to rallying religious warriors, but it is no longer generally accepted.

Osman's son Orhan captured the city of Bursa in 1326 and made it the capital. The Ottomans expanded into the Balkans in the mid-14th century, and their victory in Kosovo in 1389 effectively ended Serbian power in the region. Mehmed II ended the Byzantine Empire with the conquest of Constantinople in 1453. Further conquests by Selim I led the sultans to adopt the title of caliph, and in the 16th century, in the reign of Suleiman, the empire became a global power.

Modern scholarship holds that the empire began to decline after its defeat at the Second Siege of Vienna in 1683, though it kept a flexible economy, society and military into much of the 18th century. The Tanzimat reforms of the 19th century made the state more powerful and organised. The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 re-established a constitutional monarchy. During the First World War the empire engaged in genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Greeks. The Allies occupied and partitioned it afterwards, and the Turkish War of Independence under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk ended the sultanate in 1922.

Before the reforms of the 19th and 20th centuries the state had two dimensions, a military and a civil administration, with the sultan at the top. It first divided its territory into provinces with governors appointed by the sultan in the late 14th century, and the Vilayet Law of 1864 established the vilayet as the top of a new hierarchy. The empire granted varying levels of autonomy to its confessional communities, or millets, to manage their own affairs under Islamic law.

Mehmed II and Bayezid welcomed Jews fleeing persecution in Europe and settled them in Istanbul and Salonica. The empire's annual income quadrupled between 1523 and 1748, adjusted for inflation. Turkish was the predominant literary language, though Persian was the preferred vehicle for the imperial image. Slavery was part of Ottoman society, mostly as domestic service, and it was never abolished in the empire.
ottonian-dynasty: The family's earliest known member is the Saxon count Liudolf (d. 866), who held large estates on the Leine river west of the Harz and in the Eichsfeld of Thuringia. About 852 he and his wife Oda, with Bishop Altfrid of Hildesheim, founded Brunshausen Abbey, which after its move to Gandersheim became the family monastery and burial ground. In 869 his daughter Liutgard married Louis the Younger, son of the Carolingian king Louis the German.

Liudolf's son Otto the Illustrious was, according to the Saxon chronicler Widukind of Corvey, already a candidate for the East Frankish crown in 911, when it passed instead to the Franconian duke Conrad I. Otto died in 912, and his son Henry the Fowler succeeded him as Duke of Saxony.

Elected king in May 919, Henry won the support of the Franconian, Bavarian, Swabian and Lotharingian dukes and in 933 defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Riade. Otto I put down revolts by his brother Duke Henry I of Bavaria and his son Duke Liudolf of Swabia, reducing the dukes to royal subjects, and made the Church in Germany a base of royal power. He was crowned emperor by Pope John XII, married his heir to Theophanu, niece of the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes, and in 968 established the Archbishopric of Magdeburg.

Otto II was defeated by the Saracens at the Battle of Stilo in 982, faced the Great Slav Rising in 983 and died that year aged 28, leaving a three-year-old son for whom Empress Theophanu acted as regent. Otto III installed his confidants Bruno of Carinthia and Gerbert of Aurillac as popes and in 1000 travelled to the Congress of Gniezno; expelled from Rome in 1001, he died the next year aged 21. Henry II, of the Bavarian line, was crowned king on 7 June 1002 and emperor by Pope Benedict VIII on 14 February 1014, and founded the Bishopric of Bamberg in 1007.

Henry II's marriage to Cunigunde of Luxembourg was childless, and with his death in 1024 the dynasty became extinct. The crown passed to Conrad II of the Salian dynasty, a great-grandson of Liutgarde, daughter of Otto I; the Salians held the imperial throne until 1125. Pope Eugene III canonized Henry II in 1146. Historians disagree about how the Ottonians governed: those following Karl Leyser stress oral and ritual means, while others, such as David Bachrach, argue for the continued use of writing in administration.
ovid: Publius Ovidius Naso was born on 20 March 43 BCE in the Paelignian town of Sulmo, in an Apennine valley east of Rome, into an important equestrian family. He and his brother, who excelled at oratory, were educated in rhetoric in Rome. Their father wanted Ovid to practise law, but after his brother died at 20 Ovid renounced law and travelled to Athens, Asia Minor and Sicily. He held minor public posts but resigned, probably around 29 to 25 BCE, to pursue poetry, a decision his father apparently disapproved. He belonged to the circle of the patron Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus, claims to have heard Horace recite, and only barely met Virgil. He married three times and had divorced twice by thirty.

For the first 25 years of his career Ovid wrote mainly elegiac poetry on erotic themes. His earliest surviving work is thought to be the Heroides, letters from mythological heroines such as Penelope, Dido and Medea to their absent lovers, perhaps published in 19 BCE. He is ranked with Virgil and Horace as one of the three canonical poets of Latin literature.

He enjoyed enormous popularity, but the emperor Augustus exiled him to Tomis on the Black Sea, the capital of the newly organised province of Moesia, where he spent the last nine or ten years of his life. Ovid blamed a carmen et error, a poem and a mistake, but gave no specifics, and scholars have speculated on the cause since. His last wife helped him during his exile. He died there in 17 or 18 CE.

Ovid's best-known work is the Metamorphoses, a continuous mythological narrative in fifteen books of dactylic hexameters, which remains one of the most important sources of classical mythology. In elegiac couplets he also wrote the Ars Amatoria, or The Art of Love, and the Fasti. Scholars regard his Corinna as an invention rather than a real woman.

In the Middle Ages and the Renaissance he became one of the best known and most loved Roman poets. The French Ovide moralisé moralised the Metamorphoses and influenced Chaucer, and Arthur Golding's translation of 1567 was used in Tudor grammar schools and shaped writers such as Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare.
ovra: After the young Anteo Zamboni tried to assassinate Benito Mussolini in Bologna on 31 October 1926, the Italian government quickly passed repressive laws. All parties and associations opposed to the regime were dissolved. On 25 November 1926 the State Defence Law set up a Special Court to try those accused of being enemies of the state and restored the death penalty. The public security code enacted in 1926 specified a department of political police as a special division of the force. Its existence stayed secret until December 1930, when the official press agency Agenzia Stefani named the OVRA as a special section of the police.

Arturo Bocchini appointed the inspector Francesco Nudi as head of the OVRA; he was later replaced by Guido Leto. The organisation compiled files on around 130,000 potential subversives with the aid of approximately 100,000 informants, and by 1930 it was organising around 20,000 raids each week. About 6,000 of those it arrested, mainly communists and members of Giustizia e Libertà, are believed to have been tried by the Special Court or exiled to remote Mediterranean islands, where conditions were extremely poor. It also kept the Casellario Politico Centrale, an archive of personal profiles of known subversives.

The OVRA spied on Pope Pius XI, blackmailing priests into informing; the historian David Kertzer described its network in the Vatican as robust. Heinrich Himmler met Bocchini repeatedly, and the two police forces signed a secret protocol of cooperation on 2 April 1936. During the Second World War the OVRA was used against resistance groups in the Balkans, and in 1943 it tried to infiltrate the British Special Operations Executive with double agents. Many agents followed Mussolini to the Italian Social Republic, where they were favoured targets of communist partisans.

The OVRA was officially disbanded after the war, but a decree of 26 April 1945 ordered that the central political archive be maintained. A new police division, the Servizio Informazioni Speciali, took over its management, and many former OVRA officers were reinstated in it; its head, Inspector General Santoro, had been one of Leto's deputies. Most of the public security laws of 1931 were kept in force by the Italian Republic, and Leto himself was later reinstated as a police officer and put in charge of supervising the police academies.
oxford: Oxford is a cathedral city and the county town of Oxfordshire, at the confluence of the River Thames, known locally as the Isis, and the River Cherwell. The rivers meet south of the city centre, and they and their flood plains constrain its size. Carfax Tower is usually considered the middle of the city, where Cornmarket Street, Queen Street, St Aldate's and the High Street meet. Its name comes from the Old English Oxenaforda, ford of the oxen, a shallow crossing of the river, and the ford and the town's control of the upper Thames gave it strategic importance.

Oxford was founded in the eighth century and was granted city status in 1542. It was historically an important port on the Thames, and the Oxford-Burcot Commission of the 17th century tried to improve navigation to it. The Oxford Canal reached the city in 1790 and linked it with the industrial Midlands, bringing a steady supply of cheap coal. Salters Steamers, founded in Oxford in 1858, helped popularise pleasure boating on the Upper Thames.

Brewing was long established: several colleges had private breweries, one of them at Brasenose surviving until 1889, and in the 16th century brewing and malting appear to have been the most popular trades. By 1874 there were nine breweries in the city. Morris Motors was established in 1910, making Oxford an important centre of motor manufacturing.

Oxford is home to the University of Oxford, the oldest university in the English-speaking world, with buildings in every style of English architecture since late Anglo-Saxon. Its Ashmolean Museum, the world's first university museum, was built in 1678-1683 to house a cabinet of curiosities given to the university in 1677. Joseph Haydn received an honorary doctorate there in 1791, commemorated by three concerts at the Sheldonian Theatre; his Symphony No. 92 is nicknamed the Oxford. The city has been closely associated with religious life: it was the birthplace of the Oxford Movement in Anglicanism and of the Wesleyan Church, and the Lollard movement followed the expulsion of the theologian John Wycliffe from the university in 1381.
